title: An Ordered Collection in a Vector

blocks.text: Several values serving the same purpose

An attendance record may contain the numbers of people at several sessions. Keeping a separate variable for each session means writing repeated statements and changing the program whenever the number of sessions changes. std::vector lets us store a sequence of elements and work with it as a collection. Order is part of the data: the first session is not necessarily the one with the highest attendance.

We include <vector> and write std::vector<int> asistentes{6, 3, 8};. The <int> brackets indicate the type of each element; they are not a comparison. The braces contain the initial values, separated by commas. This vector holds three integers in the order six, three, eight. std::vector<int> is the type of this collection of integers.

size() returns the number of elements in the vector, here three. The dot means we are requesting an operation from that object. The parentheses are part of the call; we do not write asistentes.size without them.
Element type and collection size

blocks.question: What does int describe in std::vector<int> sesiones{2, 7, 4};?
options: That the vector can hold only one element.
blocks.explanation: The element type and the number of elements are different properties.

blocks.question: Use the same type as the integer literals 4 and 9: fill in only its explicit name.
blocks.explanation: The vector contains two elements of type int.

blocks.question: Predict the exact output, without adding quotation marks.
blocks.explanation: Repeated values are separate elements: eight occupies two different positions.

blocks.text: A vector can contain repeated values. size() counts elements, not distinct values. It does not automatically sort the collection either. Later, we will decide when to sort and when to preserve the original order.
Empty is also a valid state

std::vector<int> datos; creates an empty vector. It has no elements, so size() returns zero. datos.empty() asks whether it is empty and returns a bool: true when it contains no elements and false otherwise. An empty collection is not the same as a collection containing one element whose value is zero.

blocks.explanation: cout prints bool values as 1 and 0; a stored zero in una still counts as an element.

blocks.question: A vector contains {0, 0}. What does empty() return?
options: true, because all the values are zero.
false, because it contains two elements.
blocks.explanation: Emptiness depends on the absence of elements, not on their values.

blocks.text: Append with push_back

datos.push_back(5); appends a new element with value five to the end. Afterward, size() increases by one. The operation preserves the order of the existing elements. It does not mean changing the last value or reserving a space that must be filled later.

blocks.question: Predict the exact output, without adding quotation marks.
blocks.explanation: The vector that originally held one element ends up with two and is not empty.

blocks.question: Fill in only the operation name and the digit that appends nine to an empty vector.

blocks.text: Braces and parentheses answer different questions

The previous solution calls push_back(9); and the final size is one. There is another way to initialize a vector: std::vector<int> datos(3); creates three integer elements initialized to zero. In contrast, std::vector<int> datos{3}; creates one element with value three. We use braces to list values; here we use parentheses to request a number of elements.

blocks.question: Predict the exact output, without adding quotation marks.
blocks.explanation: {3} is a list containing one value; (3) requests three elements.

blocks.question: You need four quantities, all initially zero. Which declaration creates that collection?
blocks.explanation: std::vector<int> datos(4); creates four elements initialized to zero. In contrast, std::vector<int> datos{4}; creates just one element with value four.

blocks.text: Collections of text

A vector can also hold strings: std::vector<std::string> salas{"North", "Courtyard"};. You need both <vector> and <string>. Each element is a string; the two names do not automatically join into one string. We use int for counts and string for labels, just as we did with individual variables.

blocks.question: The data are labels such as "005", and their leading zeros must be preserved. Which collection is appropriate?
blocks.explanation: Labels are text; converting them into quantities would lose part of their representation.

blocks.text: In this unit's experiments, use at most twenty elements and small quantities. The goal is to check collection logic using finite loops and data defined in code.
Building a collection without placeholders

Then keep only the empty declaration and the outputs: they should display zero and one. Finally, start with one element equal to zero and explain why the collection is no longer empty.

Write one sentence distinguishing the number of records from the quantities stored in them. Seeing the number two is not enough: it must come from size(), so changes to the collection update the report.
